questions.stem: What mainly controls the size of the crystals in an igneous rock?
options: How quickly the magma or lava cooled
How much water the rock absorbed later
How old the rock is in millions of years
How far the rock is from the nearest sea
questions.explanation: Slow cooling gives atoms time to move to growing crystals, so crystals become large. Rapid cooling produces many small crystals, or glass if there is no time for crystals at all.

questions.stem: How do intrusive (plutonic) igneous rocks differ in texture from extrusive (volcanic) igneous rocks?
options: Intrusive and extrusive rocks have identical textures and differ only in their chemical composition
Intrusive rocks cool slowly underground and are coarse-grained; extrusive rocks cool fast and are fine-grained
Intrusive rocks cool fast at the surface and are fine-grained; extrusive rocks cool slowly and are coarse-grained
Intrusive rocks contain no crystals at all; extrusive rocks are made entirely of large, visible crystals
questions.explanation: Magma that crystallises deep underground is insulated by surrounding rock and cools slowly, growing large crystals. Lava at the surface loses heat quickly, giving fine crystals.

questions.stem: An igneous rock has a glassy texture with no visible crystals. What does this show?
options: The rock formed from sediment cemented by silica from groundwater
The lava cooled so quickly that crystals had no time to form
The magma cooled very slowly deep underground over millions of years
The rock was later heated and recrystallised by metamorphism
questions.explanation: Glass forms when molten rock is chilled almost instantly, so the atoms are frozen in a disordered arrangement. Obsidian is the classic example.

questions.stem: A rock contains large, well-formed feldspar crystals scattered through a fine-grained groundmass. What does this porphyritic texture indicate?
options: Weathering that enlarged some crystals after the rock reached the surface
Two stages of cooling: slow cooling at depth, then rapid cooling nearer or at the surface
One stage of very slow cooling deep underground, with the large crystals growing last of all
Two separate magmas that crystallised at exactly the same rate and then mixed
questions.explanation: The large crystals grew while the magma cooled slowly underground. The magma then rose and the remaining liquid cooled quickly, forming the fine groundmass around them.

questions.stem: A dolerite dyke is coarser-grained in its centre than at its edges, where it touches the older rock it intruded. Why?
options: The edges cooled faster against the cold surrounding rock, giving smaller crystals
The centre cooled faster because it was the part furthest from the surrounding cold rock
The edges were made of a different magma that always forms smaller crystals
The centre was weathered after intrusion, which enlarged its crystals
questions.explanation: Magma in contact with cold country rock loses heat quickly, forming fine-grained chilled margins. The insulated centre cools more slowly and grows larger crystals.

questions.stem: Igneous rocks are classified by texture and by composition. Which mineral group makes a rock felsic?
options: Abundant quartz and potassium feldspar, giving a light colour and high silica content
Abundant olivine and pyroxene, giving a dark colour and low silica content
Abundant calcite and dolomite, giving a pale colour and a strong fizzing reaction with acid
Abundant magnetite and hematite, giving a metallic lustre and red streak
questions.explanation: Felsic rocks are rich in feldspar and silica (quartz), and are light-coloured. Mafic rocks are rich in magnesium and iron minerals such as pyroxene and olivine, and are dark.

questions.stem: Which minerals are typical of a mafic igneous rock such as gabbro?
options: Calcite and shell fragments cemented together by calcium carbonate
Large crystals of quartz and pink potassium feldspar with tourmaline
Calcium-rich plagioclase feldspar and pyroxene, sometimes with olivine
Quartz, potassium feldspar and muscovite mica in roughly equal amounts
questions.explanation: Mafic rocks crystallise from low-silica magma rich in iron and magnesium, giving dark minerals such as pyroxene and olivine together with calcium-rich plagioclase.

questions.stem: How does the silica content of igneous rocks relate to their colour?
options: All igneous rocks are high in silica, so their colour depends only on age
Felsic rocks are high in silica and light; mafic rocks are low in silica and dark
Felsic rocks are low in silica and dark; mafic rocks are high in silica and light
Silica content has no relationship with colour in igneous rocks of any kind
questions.explanation: Felsic rocks such as granite and rhyolite contain roughly 70% silica, while mafic rocks such as basalt and gabbro contain about 45 to 52%. Iron- and magnesium-rich minerals make mafic rocks dark.

questions.stem: Which rock is fine-grained and mafic, and forms from lava flows?
options: Rhyolite
Basalt
Gabbro
Granite
questions.explanation: Basalt is the fine-grained, dark volcanic rock of mafic composition. Gabbro has the same composition but is coarse-grained because it cooled slowly underground.

questions.stem: Which rock has the same mafic composition as basalt but is coarse-grained?
options: Gabbro
Andesite
Rhyolite
Obsidian
questions.explanation: Gabbro is the plutonic equivalent of basalt: the same minerals, but in large crystals because it cooled slowly at depth.

questions.stem: Dolerite has a mafic composition and is medium-grained. Where does it usually form?
options: In large plutons deep in the crust, which cool more slowly than any other setting
In volcanic ash clouds, where fragments of lava cool and settle on the ground
In shallow intrusions such as dykes and sills, which cool at an intermediate rate
In lava flows at the surface, which cool more quickly than any other setting
questions.explanation: Dykes and sills are thin sheets intruded close to the surface. They cool faster than deep plutons but slower than lava, so their crystals are intermediate in size.

questions.stem: Which pair contains a fine-grained rock and a coarse-grained rock that both have an intermediate composition?
options: Andesite and diorite
Basalt and gabbro
Rhyolite and granite
Pumice and dolerite
questions.explanation: Andesite is the fine-grained volcanic rock and diorite its coarse-grained plutonic equivalent. Basalt and gabbro are mafic, and rhyolite and granite are felsic.

questions.stem: A coarse-grained rock looks speckled black and white. It is made mostly of white plagioclase feldspar and black hornblende, with little or no quartz. Which rock is it?
options: Granite
Gabbro
Andesite
Diorite
questions.explanation: Diorite is a coarse-grained intermediate rock with a salt-and-pepper look from plagioclase and hornblende. Granite would contain abundant quartz, and andesite is fine-grained.

questions.stem: Rhyolite is best described as:
options: a fine-grained, light-coloured felsic volcanic rock, the volcanic equivalent of granite
a coarse-grained, dark-coloured mafic plutonic rock, the plutonic equivalent of basalt
a glassy, black felsic rock with conchoidal fracture and no crystals at all
a rock made of compacted volcanic ash fragments thrown out by an explosive eruption
questions.explanation: Rhyolite has the same high-silica composition as granite but cooled quickly at the surface, so its crystals are too small to see easily. Glassy felsic rock is obsidian, and compacted ash is tuff.

questions.stem: Which minerals would you expect to see in a typical granite?
options: Quartz, potassium feldspar, plagioclase feldspar and mica
Olivine, pyroxene and calcium-rich plagioclase feldspar
Calcite, dolomite and fossil fragments of marine shells
Hornblende and plagioclase only, with no quartz at all
questions.explanation: Granite is a coarse-grained felsic rock made of quartz, feldspars and micas such as biotite and muscovite. Olivine and pyroxene are typical of mafic rocks.

questions.stem: A light-coloured rock has interlocking crystals 3 to 8 mm across of glassy grey quartz, pink feldspar and black mica. Which rock is it?
options: Granite
Rhyolite
Diorite
Pegmatite
questions.explanation: Visible interlocking crystals of quartz, feldspar and mica make it a coarse-grained felsic rock: granite. Rhyolite is fine-grained, diorite lacks much quartz, and pegmatite has crystals centimetres or more across.

questions.stem: A dark, dense rock from an old lava flow has crystals of plagioclase and pyroxene too small to see without a hand lens. Which rock is it?
options: Rhyolite
Dolerite
Basalt
Gabbro
questions.explanation: Fine grain and a lava flow setting show rapid surface cooling, and plagioclase with pyroxene shows mafic composition, so it is basalt. Gabbro and dolerite are coarser, and rhyolite is light and felsic.

questions.stem: Pegmatite has crystals that can be several centimetres to metres long. Why do pegmatite crystals grow so large?
options: They crystallise from water-rich residual magma in which atoms move easily to growing crystals
They crystallise from lava that cools in seconds on contact with air or seawater at the surface
They grow when volcanic ash is compacted and cemented by groundwater over millions of years
They form when sandstone is heated so strongly that its quartz grains fuse into large crystals
questions.explanation: Late-stage magma left after most crystallisation is rich in water and other volatiles. These let atoms move easily, so a few crystals grow very large. Pegmatites are usually felsic, like granite.

questions.stem: Obsidian is best described as:
options: a rock of cemented volcanic ash and fragments from an explosive eruption
a felsic volcanic glass with conchoidal fracture, formed by extremely rapid cooling
a mafic plutonic rock with large crystals of pyroxene and plagioclase feldspar
a frothy, pale glass so full of gas bubbles that it can float on water
questions.explanation: Obsidian is dark, glassy and breaks with sharp curved surfaces. It has no crystals because the high-silica lava cooled too quickly for them to form.

questions.stem: Pumice can float on water. Why?
options: It is coarse-grained granite in which the crystals have all been dissolved away
It is compacted ash in which air has been trapped between cemented fragments
It is volcanic glass full of gas bubbles (vesicles) trapped as frothy lava cooled
It is made of very light minerals such as olivine that are less dense than water
questions.explanation: Pumice forms when gas-rich felsic magma froths during an explosive eruption and is quenched, leaving glass with many vesicles. The trapped gas spaces make its overall density less than water.

questions.stem: Tuff is an igneous rock that forms from:
options: magma that cools slowly in a large chamber deep beneath a mountain range
water-rich residual magma that crystallises into very large crystals in veins
volcanic ash and rock fragments from an explosive eruption that settle and become consolidated
basaltic lava that flows gently from a long fissure and then cools slowly in a deep lava lake
questions.explanation: Tuff is a pyroclastic rock. Ash and fragments blasted out in an eruption fall or flow, then are compacted or welded together.

questions.stem: A sample of basalt contains many small, rounded holes. How did they form?
options: Crystals of salt dissolved out of the rock after it reached the sea
Burrowing animals made the holes while the basalt was still soft
Rain wore away the softest minerals after the rock was exposed
Gas bubbles were trapped as the lava cooled and solidified around them
questions.explanation: These holes are vesicles. Dissolved gas forms bubbles as lava rises and pressure falls, and bubbles near the top of a flow are frozen in place as the lava solidifies.

questions.stem: Studies of Earth's internal heat explain how magma forms beneath mid-ocean ridges and mantle plumes. What causes mantle rock to melt there?
options: Friction between the plates moving apart raises the temperature of the entire mantle below
Meteorite impacts at the ridges supply the heat needed to melt the mantle rock
Hot mantle rises and the drop in pressure lowers its melting point, so it partly melts
Seawater soaks deep into the mantle and dissolves the rock into a liquid magma
questions.explanation: This is decompression melting. The mantle is hot but mostly solid because of high pressure; as it rises the pressure falls and it begins to melt, producing basaltic magma.

questions.stem: Granites are found mainly in continental crust rather than in oceanic crust. Why?
options: Granite is too dense to stay in oceanic crust, so it sinks into the mantle
Granitic magma forms mainly by melting and differentiation of silica-rich continental crust
Granite crystallises only from basaltic lava that has been erupted onto the deep ocean floor
Granite forms when ocean water evaporates and leaves silica behind on land
questions.explanation: Continental crust is rich in silica, and melting or differentiation within it produces felsic magma that crystallises as granite. Melting of the mantle beneath oceans produces basalt.

questions.stem: In the Darling Range, dark, medium-grained mafic dykes cut across the granite. Which statement is correct?
options: The dykes are dolerite and are younger than the granite they cut
The dykes are dolerite and are older than the granite they cut
The dykes are rhyolite and are younger than the granite they cut
The dykes are pumice and are older than the granite they cut
questions.explanation: Medium-grained mafic rock in a dyke is dolerite. A dyke must be younger than the rock it cuts across, by the principle of cross-cutting relationships.
